name: Dutch East India Company
anchor: Batavia, now Jakarta, the company's headquarters on Java.
founder: Dutch trading firms merged by the States General
stopped_by: Bankruptcy, and the charter was allowed to expire
currency: The company struck its own coins
laws: Company justice under its charter, including execution of convicts
challenge: Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780 and bankruptcy
recognition: Dutch charter; treaties with Asian rulers
story:
The Dutch East India Company, known by its Dutch initials VOC, was a trading company that also ruled territory. A charter is a document in which a government grants a company special rights. On 20 March 1602 the States General, the assembly of the Dutch Republic, merged several existing trading firms into one company and gave it a 21-year monopoly on trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the Strait of Magellan.
The company could do things normally done by a state. It could wage war, negotiate treaties, strike coins, build forts, keep armies, found colonies, and imprison and execute convicts. Its investors could lose only the money they had paid in. A governor-general, a post created in 1610, ran its affairs in Asia with a Council of the Indies to advise and check him, and 17 directors in the Netherlands, the Heeren XVII, kept formal overall control.
On 30 May 1619 Jan Pieterszoon Coen stormed Jayakarta on Java and founded Batavia on its ruins as the company's headquarters. The company conquered the Banda Islands between 1609 and 1621. About 15,000 people lived there before the conquest, and about 14,000 of them were killed, enslaved or fled. Its holdings came to include Ceylon, Malacca, the Malabar coast and the Cape Colony in southern Africa.
The Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780 halved its fleet and left its net assets at zero. The board was dismissed in 1796, and the charter was allowed to expire on 31 December 1799. The Batavian Republic, the Dutch state of that time, took over the company's possessions and its debts.
mechanism: A state handed war-making, treaty-making and coinage to a private company by charter. Those powers rested on the grant, and when the company failed the state took over its land and debts.

sources.t: Dutch East India Company, Wikipedia

name: English East India Company
anchor: Calcutta, now Kolkata, where the company set up a base after 1690. Its headquarters was East India House in London.
founder: Merchants of London, chartered by Queen Elizabeth I
laws: Civil and criminal jurisdiction over areas it acquired
recognition: English royal charter; sovereignty passed to the Crown in 1858
story:
The East India Company began as a group of London merchants. On 31 December 1600 Queen Elizabeth I gave them a charter, a document granting special rights, with a 15-year monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the Straits of Magellan.
Around 1670 a series of five acts under Charles II gave the company the right to acquire territory on its own, mint money, command forts and troops, form alliances, make war and peace, and hold civil and criminal jurisdiction, meaning the authority to try cases, over the areas it acquired.
On 23 June 1757 at Plassey, Robert Clive's force of about 800 soldiers and 2,200 Indian soldiers known as sepoys defeated Siraj ud-Daula, the Nawab of Bengal, helped by a prior plot with the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar. In 1765 the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the company the diwani, the right to collect and manage the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The Great Bengal famine of 1770 is estimated to have killed about 10 million people. At its peak the company's three armies totalled about 260,000 soldiers, about twice the size of the British Army at certain times.
By 1858 the company, or princely states tied to it by treaty, ruled most of modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh along with Lower Burma. It had given up its commercial assets in India in 1833. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 nationalised it, and the Crown took over its possessions, its administration and its armed forces. The company was formally dissolved on 1 June 1874.
mechanism: A company held trading rights from its own state and revenue rights from a local emperor, and it enforced both with its own army. Its home parliament could take all of this over by passing a statute, and in 1858 it did.

sources.t: East India Company, Wikipedia

name: Royal Niger Company
anchor: Lokoja, at the meeting of the Niger and Benue rivers in Nigeria.
recognition: British royal charter of 1886, with over 400 treaties with local leaders
cost: £865,000 paid by Britain for its territories
story:
The Royal Niger Company grew out of British firms trading on the Niger River in what is now Nigeria. George Goldie argued that the surviving firms should merge, and by 1879 he had helped combine them as the United African Company. It later became the National African Company.
In July 1886 it received a royal charter, a grant of special rights from the British Crown, and became the Royal Niger Company, with Lord Aberdare as governor and Goldie as vice-governor. Over 400 treaties with local leaders obliged local people to trade only with or through the company's agents. British consuls later turned these into general treaties. The company's monopoly and treaties helped Britain resist French and German calls at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 to open Niger trade to all.
The charter was revoked in 1899. On 1 January 1900 the company transferred its territories to the British government for £865,000. The land, together with the Niger Coast Protectorate, became the protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria, which were united as Nigeria in 1914. The business carried on as the Niger Company, then the United Africa Company from 1929, and it came under the control of Unilever in the 1930s.
mechanism: Treaties signed by a private firm with local rulers gave its home state a claim against European rivals. Once the state wanted direct rule, it revoked the charter and paid for the territory.

sources.t: Royal Niger Company, Wikipedia

name: Hudson's Bay Company as a government
aka: The Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay
anchor: Western shore of Hudson Bay, where the company built its forts.
founder: London investors, with Prince Rupert of the Rhine as first governor
laws: Company-controlled courts, such as the Court of Assiniboia
recognition: English royal charter; sovereignty lay with the Crown
story:
On 2 May 1670 King Charles II gave a royal charter to a group called the Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay. It granted them sole trade over Rupert's Land, the region drained by all rivers flowing into Hudson Bay. That area was about 3.86 million square kilometres, more than a third of modern Canada, and its exact boundaries were unknown at the time.
For about 200 years the company was the government of that land in practice. It built forts on the bay, and later posts inland, and it set prices through a list called the Standard of Trade, which used a prime beaver pelt, the Made Beaver, as its unit of value. It issued its own paper money from 1820 to 1870 and controlled courts, such as the Court of Assiniboia. In 1821 the British government forced it to merge with its violent rival, the North West Company, and a licence then extended its reach to the Arctic Ocean and the Pacific.
In 1869 the company turned down a US offer of 10 million Canadian dollars and agreed to return Rupert's Land to Britain, which passed it to Canada and lent Canada £300,000 to pay the company. The company kept its trading posts and one-twentieth of the fertile land. The Deed of Surrender took effect on 15 July 1870.
The company survived as a retailer. It filed for creditor protection on 7 March 2025, its stores had closed by 1 June 2025, and its royal charter was auctioned in the liquidation.
mechanism: A trade monopoly from the Crown became government in practice because no other authority was on the ground. The sovereignty stayed with the Crown, so the company could give up the land only through Britain.

sources.t: Hudson's Bay Company, Wikipedia

name: British South Africa Company
anchor: Fort Salisbury, now Harare, where the Pioneer Column stopped in 1890.
stopped_by: Responsible government in Southern Rhodesia in 1923; an agreement ending its rule in Northern Rhodesia in 1924
challenge: Jameson Raid and the Matabele Wars
cost: £4 million paid in 1964 to end its mineral rights
story:
The British South Africa Company was formed by Cecil Rhodes and received a royal charter effective 20 December 1889. A royal charter is a grant of special rights from the Crown. This one first ran for 25 years. It let the company make treaties with African rulers to secure public order, subject to British approval, and form banks, own and grant land, and raise a police force. In return it was to develop the territory, respect African laws, allow free trade and respect all religions.
The company relied on the Rudd Concession, a mining grant obtained from the Ndebele king Lobengula. A group of settlers known as the Pioneer Column reached Fort Salisbury in 1890, and a company Administrator was appointed that October. Company police fought in the First and Second Matabele Wars, and uprisings followed in 1896.
After the Jameson Raid, Rhodes accepted full responsibility and he and Alfred Beit were removed as directors in June 1896. The police were renamed the British South Africa Police and reported from then on to the British High Commissioner, and Britain tightened its oversight of the company.
Company rule ended in Southern Rhodesia in 1923, when that territory gained responsible government, and in Northern Rhodesia on 1 April 1924. The company kept mineral rights in Northern Rhodesia and collected royalties until 1964. On 23 October 1964, just before Zambian independence, it agreed to give them up for £4 million, paid half by Britain and half by Zambia.
mechanism: The charter let a private company raise police and govern, with the British government keeping the right to approve and oversee. Mineral rights outlasted the right to govern by 40 years.

sources.t: British South Africa Company, Wikipedia

name: Imperial British East Africa Company
anchor: Mombasa, Kenya, the centre of the company's operations.
story:
The Imperial British East Africa Company was a British firm led by the Scottish businessman William Mackinnon. It was incorporated in London on 18 April 1888, and Queen Victoria gave it a royal charter on 6 September that year. A treaty of 1886 had given Germany the coast of what is now Tanzania and left Britain access to the area of Kenya and Uganda. The company worked from Mombasa and its harbour, with an administrative office in Shimoni, about 80 kilometres to the south.
The company sent Frederick Lugard inland to build a fortified post on Kampala Hill in Uganda. A civil war broke out there in January 1892 and Lugard took part on the company's behalf. The cost of the conflict, added to existing trouble over customs, nearly bankrupted the company.
The British government then took over. It declared a protectorate over Uganda in 1894 and formed the East Africa Protectorate, later Kenya, in 1895. A protectorate is a territory run under the protection and control of a stronger state. Dates for the end of the company vary, with administrative rights passing in 1893 and the company listed as defunct in 1896.
mechanism: A chartered company carried the cost of occupying territory until it could not pay, and then its home state took direct control.

name: Gadsden Purchase
anchor: Southern Arizona around Tucson, within the land bought from Mexico.
story:
The Gadsden Purchase was the sale by Mexico to the United States of 76,800 square kilometres of what is now southern Arizona and south-western New Mexico, the land south of the Gila River and west of the Rio Grande. James Gadsden, the US minister to Mexico, negotiated it with Mexico's president, Antonio López de Santa Anna, starting on 25 September 1853, and the treaty was drawn up at the end of that December.
The United States wanted a flatter southern route for a railway to California. The purchase also settled uncertainty about the border. The first price offered was $15 million. The US Senate rejected the original text on 17 April 1854 by falling three votes short of the two-thirds it needed, and then on 25 April passed a revised version by 33 to 12 that cut more than 10,000 square miles and lowered the price to $10 million. Santa Anna accepted the changes.
The land was added to New Mexico Territory, and Fort Buchanan was built to control it. Arizona Territory was created in 1863 and Arizona became a state in 1912. The disputes over slavery stalled a southern railway until the Southern Pacific reached Tucson in 1880 and completed its route in 1883. Mexican opinion of the sale was negative, and Mexican historians still view it critically.
mechanism: Two governments moved sovereignty and a border by treaty for money. People's ordinary legal position changed with the flag, and the treaty needed approval from the US Senate by a two-thirds vote.

name: Alaska Purchase
anchor: Sitka, Alaska, where the transfer ceremony was held.
founder: United States, through William H. Seward
story:
The Alaska Purchase was the sale of Russia's colony in North America to the United States. William H. Seward, the US Secretary of State, and Eduard de Stoeckl, a Russian diplomat, signed the treaty at 4 in the morning on 30 March 1867 after an all-night session. The price was $7.2 million for 1,518,800 square kilometres, about 2 cents an acre. A list of territory purchases gives a slightly larger area.
Russia needed money after its defeat in the Crimean War. The colony was hard to defend and could easily have been taken by British forces from Canada, and the sea otter population it relied on had nearly died out. The US Senate ratified the treaty on 9 April by 37 votes to 2.
The treaty took effect on 18 October 1867, when the Russian flag was lowered at Sitka and the American flag raised. Nearly all Russians left, and most returned home by 1869. Seward estimated about 60,000 inhabitants, of whom about 50,000 were Inuit or Alaska Natives living outside Russian control, so most people in the territory had been governed by neither side before the sale.
Alaska was run as a department, then a district and then a territory, and it became a state in 1959.
mechanism: A state sold its claim to a colony by treaty. The buyer received what the seller claimed, including authority over Indigenous peoples who had never been under the seller's actual control.

name: Louisiana Purchase
anchor: The Cabildo in New Orleans, where France transferred the city to the United States.
founder: United States, through Robert Livingston and James Monroe
story:
The Louisiana Purchase was the sale by France to the United States of a claim to about 2,140,000 square kilometres of North America, west of the Mississippi River. Robert Livingston and James Monroe signed the treaty for the United States in Paris on 30 April 1803 with François Barbé-Marbois, the French treasury minister.
France had ceded the territory to Spain in a secret treaty of 1762 and got it back in a secret treaty of 1800. Napoleon then gave up on a New World empire because the revolt in Saint-Domingue was not put down and war with Britain looked close. The price was 80 million francs, or $15 million. The United States took on up to $3.75 million of French debts to its own citizens and paid the rest in bonds, which it financed through British and Dutch banks. With interest the cost came to about $23.3 million.
The US constitution says nothing directly about buying territory. President Thomas Jefferson considered an amendment and was persuaded by his cabinet that the treaty power was enough. The Senate approved the treaty by 24 votes to 7 on 20 October 1803.
The treaty was negotiated without consulting the Native nations living on the land, who had not ceded it to any colonial power. What the United States bought, in effect, was the sole right among outsiders to obtain Indian lands. Later treaties and settlements for those lands cost it about $2.6 billion through 2012.
mechanism: A seller can pass on only what it holds. France sold its claim against other colonial powers, and the people on the land had to be dealt with separately, often through decades of further treaties and force.

name: Sale of the Danish West Indies
aka: Treaty of the Danish West Indies
anchor: Saint Thomas, one of the three islands sold.
story:
In 1916 Denmark sold three Caribbean islands, Saint Croix, Saint John and Saint Thomas, to the United States for $25 million in gold. The treaty was signed in New York on 4 August 1916 by the Danish minister Constantin Brun and the US Secretary of State Robert Lansing. The islands cover about 400 square kilometres. The islands are now the US Virgin Islands.
Earlier deals had failed. A treaty of 1867 for $7.5 million was ratified in Denmark and never by the US Senate. A deal of 1902 for $5 million failed when the upper house of the Danish parliament tied 32 to 32. During the First World War, Americans feared that Germany might seize the islands if it invaded Denmark, and the islands lay close to the Panama Canal.
Danish voters took part in a referendum on 14 December 1916 and the Danish parliament ratified the treaty on 22 December. The islands changed hands on 31 March 1917, now a public holiday called Transfer Day. As part of the deal Lansing declared that the United States would not object to Denmark extending its interests to the whole of Greenland.
mechanism: A sale by treaty that came with a side declaration on a different territory. The islanders' own status was decided by the two governments and voters in Denmark.

name: Mexican Cession
anchor: Guadalupe Hidalgo, near Mexico City, where the treaty was signed.
challenge: Land grant disputes into the 21st century
cost: $15 million plus $3.25 million in debts taken over
story:
The Mexican Cession was the transfer of about 1.36 million square kilometres from Mexico to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848. It ended the Mexican-American War and covered present-day California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and parts of New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming, about 55 per cent of Mexico's territory.
The treaty mixes a peace settlement with a sale. The United States paid $15 million in yearly instalments of $3 million and took over $3.25 million that Mexico owed to US citizens.
People living there had one year to choose between US and Mexican citizenship, and over 90 per cent chose US citizenship. The treaty protected existing property rights. The US Senate removed the article that would have guaranteed land grants made by Spain and Mexico. A later protocol confirmed those grants under Mexican law, the United States later ignored it, and disputes over them continued into the 21st century.
mechanism: A payment attached to a cession at the end of a war. Private land titles were meant to survive the change of sovereign, and their protection depended on the buyer's Senate and courts.

name: Sale of Florida
anchor: Northern Florida, within the land transferred.
founder: United States, through John Quincy Adams, and Spain, through Luis de Onís
cost: About $5 million paid to US claimants
story:
Under the Adams-Onís Treaty, signed in Washington on 22 February 1819, Spain gave East and West Florida to the United States. John Quincy Adams negotiated for the United States and the Spanish ambassador, Luis de Onís, for Spain. The treaty also drew a border running from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific.
The money did not go to Spain. The United States agreed to compensate its own citizens for losses they said Spain had caused, and a commission paid out about $5 million before it closed in 1824. A list of territory purchases counts this as the price of about 200,000 square kilometres.
The US Senate approved the treaty unanimously two days after signing. Spain delayed until October 1820, the Senate voted again, and the treaty took effect on 22 February 1821.
mechanism: A cession paid for by cancelling claims. The buyer settled debts owed to its own citizens, so the sale could be counted as a purchase with no cash passing to the seller.

name: Cession of the Philippines
anchor: Manila, Philippines.
challenge: The First Philippine Republic resisted American sovereignty
story:
By the Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 December 1898 after the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded the Philippine Islands to the United States for $20 million. The islands cover about 300,000 square kilometres.
Spain's hold was already contested. Philippine revolutionaries had declared independence from Spain on 12 June 1898. Felipe Agoncillo, a lawyer representing the First Philippine Republic, was denied any part in the talks.
Fighting between Filipino and American forces broke out in Manila on 4 February 1899. Two days later the US Senate approved the treaty by 57 votes to 27, just above the two-thirds needed. The treaty took effect on 11 April 1899.
mechanism: Two outside states set the sovereignty of a territory by treaty and left out the government its people had declared. Recognition by those two states did not settle the matter on the ground, which went to war.

name: Sale of Saint Barthélemy
anchor: Gustavia, Saint Barthélemy.
story:
Saint Barthélemy is a Caribbean island of 21 square kilometres that passed between owners several times. The Order of Saint John, a Catholic knightly order, held it in the 1600s, and the French West India Company bought it in 1665 with the order's other Caribbean holdings.
In 1784 King Louis XVI of France traded the island to Sweden for trading privileges in Gothenburg. The Swedes named the town of Gustavia after their king, Gustav III, and made it a free port, one where goods paid no customs duties. The colony lasted nearly a century.
After a status referendum in 1877, Sweden sold the island back to France, and it returned on 16 March 1878. A list of territory purchases gives the price as 320,000 French francs. Today it is a French overseas collectivity, a territory with its own council that remains part of France. It separated from Guadeloupe in 2007 and left the European Union in 2012. The 2023 census counted 10,660 residents.
mechanism: A small territory moved between states by trade and by sale, with a local vote before the second transfer. Later changes to its status came through French law.

name: Transfer of Gwadar to Pakistan
anchor: Gwadar, on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast.
founder: Pakistan and the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman
cost: Accounts differ: 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees, or a contribution of about $3 million
story:
Gwadar is a port town on the Arabian Sea. It was an overseas possession of the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman from 1783 to 1958, a link that began with a grant from the Khan of Kalat to Sultan bin Ahmad.
On 8 September 1958 Oman handed Gwadar to Pakistan. Prime Minister Feroz Khan Noon and his wife, Viqar-un-Nisa Noon, are credited with convincing the British government to allow the handover. Sources disagree on the money. One Wikipedia list gives a price of 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees and an area of 15,210 square kilometres, and Wikipedia's article on Gwadar gives no official price and mentions a contribution of about $3 million from Prince Karim Aga Khan IV.
Gwadar became part of Makran district and a district of its own in 1977. Construction of the first phase of Gwadar Port began in 2007 at a cost of $248 million, and in 2013 the state-owned China Overseas Port Holdings acquired the port.
mechanism: A state transferred an overseas possession by agreement for money, with a third state's consent. Later the buyer gave a foreign state-owned company the port, which involves control of a business and leaves sovereignty with Pakistan.

name: Return of Elten and Selfkant
anchor: Elten, on the Rhine near Emmerich, Germany.
story:
After the Second World War the Netherlands took small pieces of German land. On 23 April 1949 Dutch troops occupied about 69 square kilometres, with almost 10,000 inhabitants in all. The largest parts were the town of Elten on the Rhine, with 3,235 people, and Selfkant near Sittard, with 5,665.
West Germany began negotiating for their return in March 1957. A treaty signed in The Hague on 8 April 1960 had West Germany pay 280 million German marks for the return of Elten, Selfkant and the village of Suderwick. The payment was described as compensation. The land went back on 1 August 1963, except for a hill of about 3 square kilometres near Wyler that the Netherlands kept.
Before the border moved, traders stored coffee and butter in the towns about to change country. At midnight the goods were on the other side of the border without having paid import tax. The night is remembered as Butter Night. It is the most recent sale in a Wikipedia list of territory purchases.
mechanism: Land taken after a war was returned by treaty for a payment. It shows that a border change also moves customs and tax law in a single instant.

name: Norway's sale of the Isle of Man and the Hebrides
anchor: The Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland.
cost: 4,000 marks sterling and a yearly 100 marks
story:
In 1266 Scotland bought the Isle of Man, the Hebrides, Kintyre and the islands of the Firth of Clyde from Norway for 4,000 marks sterling and a yearly 100 marks. The area was about 8,000 square kilometres.
A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.
mechanism: Two rulers or states settled this by agreement, and the people living there had the new ruler's law applied to them from then on.

A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.

sources.t: List of territory purchased by a sovereign nation from another sovereign nation, Wikipedia
